scoreNote: Strong-adequate (4.5): a recommendation response that grants the value of early support while warning against rigid early selection; two developed examples with analysis, controlled prose at about 400 words on a memorable First and Second skeleton.

sentences.text: Many great musicians, athletes, and scientists showed their gifts when they were still very young.
Some people recommend that society should identify children with special talents early and provide training to develop those gifts.
I agree that early encouragement can be valuable, but I believe that selecting and labelling children too early would do real harm.

sections.role: Body 1 — The value of early support

sentences.text: First, in many cases, giving talented children early training helps them reach their full potential.
Skills such as music, dance, and gymnastics are far easier to master when serious training begins in childhood.
For example, most world-class violinists and ballet dancers started intense practice long before they reached their teenage years.
This shows that early support can turn raw natural ability into genuine and lasting excellence.
A child whose talent is noticed and nurtured may gain a confidence and sense of purpose that last a lifetime.
Without such support, gifted children from poorer families in particular may never discover what they could have achieved.
Where ability is clear and the child is willing, early training is plainly a good thing.

sections.role: Body 2 — The dangers of early selection

sentences.text: Second, however, identifying and separating talented children too early carries serious risks.
Young children change quickly, so a gift that seems obvious at six may fade, while a slow starter may bloom much later.
Consider a child wrongly judged ordinary at an early age, who is then denied the chances quietly given to the chosen few.
Such early labelling can crush the confidence of children who are simply developing at a slower natural pace.
A system focused only on a talented minority may also neglect the many ordinary children who deserve a good education too.
Pushing very young children into intense training can rob them of play, friendship, and an ordinary childhood.
For these reasons, any early selection must be gentle, flexible, and always open to second chances.
In conclusion, helping talented children develop their gifts early can be genuinely worthwhile.
But rigidly identifying and separating them too soon risks unfairness, mistakes, and a lost childhood.
The wiser approach is to nurture talent wherever it appears while never closing the door on children who develop later.
